justification: DQ-54: git exports GIT_DIR and GIT_INDEX_FILE to its hooks and they OVERRIDE cwd, so a script that carefully passes cwd=<repo> and is then invoked from a hook reads a DIFFERENT repository — exit 0, no warning. Two of the sites decide which .env supplies credentials (DATABASE_URL, an API key) and one DELETES files. The tracker logged this on 2026-08-08 as prose naming three call sites; four days later the same class caused a second incident and the highest-consequence site was still unscrubbed. This replaces the prose with a ratchet, which then found four more sites nobody had named.

falsifiable_check.fails_when: Any script in scripts/ runs git with an explicit cwd= and no env=. It is an AST scan, not a grep: it walks every subprocess call, keeps those whose argv literal starts with "git" AND that pin a cwd, and asserts each also pins an env. Proven able to fail before it passed — its first run went 4 failed / 242 passed, naming prove_qa_report_binding.py, prune_qa_reports.py, sol_common.py and sweep_absence_negative_tests.py, none of which DQ-54 had listed. After the fixes: 246/246. It also checks the four inherits-by-design exemptions still pass no cwd, so an exemption cannot quietly become a licence for the defect.
falsifiable_check.external_authority: git decides, and its own documented behaviour is the authority: GIT_DIR and GIT_INDEX_FILE override cwd. DQ-54 recorded this measured live — with GIT_DIR pointed elsewhere, git log, git rev-parse --git-common-dir and git ls-files run from a worktree all answered about the other repository, exit 0, no warning. The canonical scrub already existed at scripts/qa_report_path.py:103 and is the thing being adopted, not invented.

pre_impl.existing_data: DQ-54 in .claude/DATA_QUALITY_TRACKER.md, logged 2026-08-08, report-only by instruction, naming cross_review.py (2 calls), validate_schema_contract.py:408 and qa_gate.py:1385, and prescribing 'one shared git_env() helper at three call sites'. The helper already existed at qa_report_path.py:103, already used correctly by qa_gate.py:1306 and doc_claims.py. The prior incident it cites is real: on 2026-08-07 a fixture git commit landed on the real worktree's branch and replaced its index.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: Two, and both changed the work. First, I assumed the tracker's site list was the scope. It was not — the AST ratchet found FOUR more scripts with the same shape, so 'three call sites' was an undercount of more than half. A hand-enumerated list of a defect class is a snapshot, and this one had already drifted in four days. Second, I assumed the scrub I wrote in #927 was correct and merely needed copying. It was over-strict: it dropped every GIT_* including GIT_ASKPASS, GIT_SSH and GIT_SSH_COMMAND, which configure how git AUTHENTICATES rather than which repository it reads, and which the canonical helper deliberately keeps. Adopting the shared helper fixed my own bug as a side effect. Third: I assumed 'has an env= kwarg' was a sufficient check. It is not — env=os.environ.copy() passes it and scrubs nothing, and tightening it to require git_env() immediately surfaced two more scripts whose inline comprehensions were correct but carried the same over-strict auth-var bug.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: No new helper. qa_report_path.git_env() already existed and is now imported by six scripts instead of one. The only new file is the ratchet test. doc_claims.py keeps its deliberate second copy, which qa_report_path's own docstring explains as avoiding a heavy import — left alone rather than 'tidied' into a dependency.

functions.name: test_git_calls_that_pin_cwd_also_pin_env
functions.input: every *.py in scripts/, parsed to an AST, excluding the two modules that define the scrub itself
functions.output: a failure naming the file and line numbers of any git call that pins cwd without env, plus the exact fix line; parametrised per file so the report names the offender rather than a single opaque failure
functions.if_none: no offenders means the shape is absent from scripts/ — NOT that the class is empty, since a dynamically assembled call or one reaching git through a wrapper is invisible to a source scan; that limit is stated in the module docstring rather than left implied

functions.name: test_the_exemption_list_is_still_true
functions.input: the four scripts exempted because they pass no cwd and genuinely want the hook's repository
functions.output: a failure if any of them later grows a cwd=, because at that moment the exemption stops describing them and starts excusing them
functions.if_none: skips if a listed file no longer exists, so deleting a script does not fail the suite for the wrong reason

break_it.scenario: The scrub also removes the variables that configure git AUTHENTICATION, so credential helpers and signed operations break in environments that rely on them.
break_it.what_happens: git ls-remote in prune_qa_reports.py, and any future networked call, starts failing to authenticate. prune treats an unanswerable ls-remote as 'unknown' and refuses to delete, so it degrades to inert rather than destructive — but a fetch elsewhere would simply fail.
break_it.how: The canonical helper keeps GIT_ASKPASS, GIT_SSH and GIT_SSH_COMMAND precisely because they configure how git authenticates, not which repo it reads. This is exactly the bug in the local scrub I wrote in #927, which dropped all three; adopting the shared helper removes it. Pinned by test_the_shared_helper_keeps_auth_variables, which sets all seven variables and asserts three survive and four are dropped. Confirmed live: prune's ls-remote still resolves 276 branches.

break_it.scenario: A script reaches git without matching the AST pattern — argv built dynamically, a shell string, or a call through a helper the scan cannot follow.
break_it.what_happens: It stays exposed while the suite is green, and the ratchet's green becomes false assurance, which is worse than no ratchet because it stops people looking.
break_it.how: Not mitigated and stated as a limit in the module docstring rather than left implied: this pins the shape that actually recurred twice, it does not prove the class is empty. A semantic check would need to resolve argv values across the call graph. The mitigation available today is that the two known-dangerous idioms — a literal ['git', ...] argv with cwd, and the --git-common-dir env-discovery pattern — are both covered.

break_it.scenario: sol_common.py and sweep_absence_negative_tests.py gained a sys.path.insert plus an import at module scope, and one of them is imported in a context where scripts/ is not importable — so the import raises and the module dies.
break_it.what_happens: cross_review.py imports sol_common, so a failure there takes out the cross-review tool entirely; the failure is loud rather than silent, but it would break the reviewer that found two real defects for me today.
break_it.how: Both insert their own directory on sys.path immediately before the import, so they do not depend on a caller having done it. Verified by executing them, not just importing: sweep prints its --help and exits 0, prune completes a dry run, and the full 4,482-test suite collects and passes, which exercises the import path under pytest's own loader too.

break_it.scenario: The exemption list rots: one of the four inherits-by-design scripts later grows a cwd=, and the exemption silently licenses the defect it was meant to describe.
break_it.what_happens: That script starts reading the wrong repository under a hook, and the ratchet says nothing because the file is on the allowlist.
break_it.how: The exemption is treated as a claim and verified rather than trusted: test_the_exemption_list_is_still_true parses each of the four and fails if any git call pins a cwd, telling the reader to either drop the cwd or leave the list and pass env=git_env().

break_it.scenario: The ratchet accepts ANY env= keyword, so env=os.environ.copy() satisfies it while scrubbing nothing.
break_it.what_happens: A developer 'fixes' a flagged call by passing the unmodified environment. The ratchet goes green, the hook's GIT_DIR still overrides cwd, and the command still reads the wrong repository — an open defect converted into a green tick, which is worse than no ratchet because it stops people looking.
break_it.how: Cross-review finding on push, verified and correct. The check now inspects the env VALUE and requires a call to git_env(), accepting both spellings in use (bare and qa_report_path-qualified). Proven by planting exactly the reviewer's example — env=os.environ.copy() in sol_common.py — which takes the suite from 246 passed to a named failure on that file, then reverting.
break_it.repro: python -m pytest tests/test_git_env_ratchet.py -q   # then plant env=os.environ.copy() on any flagged call

break_it.scenario: The auth-variable test writes GIT_* directly and pops them in a finally, destroying values the pytest process inherited.
break_it.what_happens: This suite is run BY pre-push, which exports GIT_DIR and GIT_INDEX_FILE. Unconditionally popping them strips the hook environment for every test that runs afterwards, so a later test containing an unscrubbed git call passes — silently masking the exact defect this file exists to detect. Any real GIT_SSH_COMMAND is discarded too.
break_it.how: Cross-review finding, and the more serious of the two because the test would have sabotaged its own suite. Rewritten onto pytest's monkeypatch fixture, which restores prior values AND prior absence exactly. The reason it matters here rather than in a normal test file is stated in the docstring so the next person does not 'simplify' it back.

mutation_analysis: The mutation ran itself: the ratchet's FIRST execution was against unpatched code and went 4 failed / 242 passed, naming four scripts the tracker never listed. That is the strongest form of this evidence — the test failed on real pre-existing defects before any of them were fixed, so it cannot be a test written to match code that already passed. Re-running after the patches gives 246/246. The auth-preservation test was checked the same way: it fails against #927's local scrub, which dropped GIT_ASKPASS/GIT_SSH/GIT_SSH_COMMAND, and passes against the shared helper. The weak version of this work would have been patching the three sites the tracker named and declaring DQ-54 closed; that would have left four scripts exposed, including the one that deletes files.
residual_risk: The ratchet is a source scan and cannot see a git call assembled dynamically or reached through a wrapper — stated in the docstring, not hidden. doc_claims.py keeps a second copy of git_env by design, so the codebase has two definitions and a future edit could drift them apart; consolidating would introduce the heavy import the docstring exists to avoid, so it is a recorded trade-off rather than an oversight. Nothing here addresses hook-invoked scripts OUTSIDE scripts/, and .githooks/ shell scripts are not scanned at all. DQ-54's own status line in the tracker still says 'Open — report-only by instruction'; this PR does the fix but does not edit the tracker, so that row needs updating separately. The two flood scripts were already scrubbing correctly via an inline comprehension; they were converted to the shared helper for consistency with DQ-54's 'one shared helper' and to pick up the auth-variable preservation, not because they were broken.

post_merge.db_reset: No. No schema, data or query change. One of the fixed sites influences which .env is loaded, so if anything the DB targeting becomes more correct, not less.
post_merge.secrets: None read or written by this change. sol_common.py's fix makes the API-key .env lookup resolve against the intended repository rather than a hook's.
post_merge.other_repo: No. Single repository — which is the entire point of the fix.
post_merge.manual_verify: Yes, one cheap check: run any push from a worktree and confirm the pre-push cross-review still produces findings rather than erroring, since cross_review.py and its sol_common dependency both changed and both are exercised only at push time.
